overview.summary: Learn to work well with AI assistants and agents: decide what to hand over, brief them clearly, break work into checked steps, and check everything before you use it. Eleven hands-on modules use free tools (Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude, any one) and Indian workplace cases, each with a short interactive workbook. Then a final test, and a portfolio project with a mentor: an AI-assisted workflow for a real small organisation.
overview.audience: students and graduates in any field who want to use AI well in college, in an internship and at work; no coding needed
outcomes: Decide which parts of a task to hand to an AI assistant or agent, and which to keep
Brief an AI with a goal, context, audience, limits, an example and an output format
Check AI output for wrong facts, sources and numbers, and keep a verification log
Protect personal and confidential data, and set approval points and limits so hidden instructions can’t make an agent pay, send or delete without a person’s yes
Build and test a simple no-code AI workflow with a human check
Disclose AI use honestly and own the result you hand in

items.statement: Before I use an AI answer, I ask myself whether the AI could actually know that fact.
When a saved template or a checklist would do a job, I use that instead of an AI tool.
If an AI answer sounds sure of itself, I take it as correct.
When I ask an AI for something, I include the facts it can’t know, such as prices or dates.
When an AI reply isn’t what I wanted, I tell it exactly what to change.
I send an AI a one-line request and use whatever comes back.
I open a source an AI gives me before I repeat what it says.
I work out a number again myself before I use one an AI gave me.
To check an AI answer, I ask the AI whether it is sure.
Before I paste work data into an AI tool, I remove names, phone numbers and other personal details.
I find out whether my college or employer allows a tool before I put their files into it.
I paste other people’s messages into AI tools when it saves me time.
When I hand in work, I say what AI did in it.
When I’m learning something new, I try it myself before I ask AI.
I let AI write the parts of an assignment I find hardest.
I split a big piece of work into smaller steps before I start.
In a long task, I check each step before I move on to the next.
I ask an AI to do a whole project in one request.
When a question is about my own data, I give the AI the file instead of asking from memory.
When an AI works from a file I gave it, I check at least one of its numbers against the file.
I give apps and AI tools every permission they ask for, so they work smoothly.
When I do the same task every week, I look for a way to set it up once.
Before I rely on something that runs by itself, I test it with unusual inputs.
Once something I set up is working, I stop checking on it.

modules.title: Assistants, workflows and agents
modules.summary: What AI assistants, workflows and agents are, what each can and can't do, and the loop you'll use all programme: decide, brief, check, own.
modules.outcome: Say whether a task needs a chat assistant, a fixed workflow or an agent, and name what you would check before using the result.

learn.title: What an AI assistant really does
learn.body:
An AI assistant such as Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude runs on a large language model (LLM). An LLM learns from huge amounts of text to predict the likely next words. That is why it writes so fluently. It is also why it can be wrong while sounding sure. A likely sentence is not always a true one.

Worked example. Rohan asks an assistant, “What time does our college library close?” It replies “8 pm” with full confidence. It has never seen his college’s notice. It guessed a likely answer.

Assistants are good at drafts, summaries, explanations, ideas and rewording. They are weak at facts they can’t look up, exact counts, and anything about your situation you haven’t told them. Some can search the web or read a file you attach. That helps, but you still check.

learn.title: Workflows and agents: who decides the steps
learn.body:
In a workflow, a person fixes the steps in advance and the AI does some of them. In an agent, the AI decides its own next steps and which tools to use until the job is done. Tools include web search, files, a browser or other apps.

Worked example. A Jaipur coaching centre wants replies to parents’ enquiries. As a workflow: each new form entry goes to the AI, which drafts a reply from the fee sheet, and a staff member approves it. As an agent: told “fill our empty seats this week”, the AI might search, write to parents and post offers on its own.

The agent is more flexible. It also costs more, runs slower, and its mistakes can add up step by step. Anthropic, an AI company, advises the simplest set-up that works, and agents only when the steps can’t be planned ahead.

learn.title: The loop for this whole programme
learn.body:
Each time you use AI for real work, run four steps.
Decide: should AI do this at all, and which part?
Brief: tell it the goal, the facts and the format.
Check: test facts, numbers and sources before you use anything.
Own: your name goes on the result, so you answer for it.

Worked example. Sana, an intern at a Kochi clinic, needs a poster on preventing dengue. Decide: AI can draft the words, but a doctor must approve health advice. Brief: audience, languages, poster size. Check: she compares every tip with the health advice the clinic already uses. Own: she shows the doctor and notes that AI drafted it.

The common mistake is jumping from brief to send. In Microsoft’s Work Trend Index 2026, AI users in India ranked checking the quality of AI output as the top skill.

tasks.title: Test where an assistant is strong and weak
tasks.prompt:
Open any free AI assistant (Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude) on your phone. Send these three prompts, one at a time.
A: Rewrite this notice for first-year students in simple English, under 60 words: “All students are hereby informed that the submission of the project synopsis must be completed on or before the stipulated deadline, failing which marks shall be deducted.”
B: What is the last date to pay fees at [your college’s name] this semester?
C: How many words are in this sentence: “Our kirana store opens at seven and closes at ten every day except Sunday.”
Hand in a table with four columns: the prompt, the AI’s answer, your verdict (right, wrong or can’t tell), and how you checked it.
tasks.hint: For C, count by hand: the sentence has 14 words. For B, compare with your college’s notice or website. If the AI gave a date with no source you can open, mark it “can’t tell” until you check.
tasks.after: A good table shows A done well: simpler, under 60 words, with the deadline and the penalty kept. B is marked “can’t tell” until checked against the college’s own notice. C is counted by hand: 14. The point: a fluent answer still needs a check, and the right check depends on the task.

tasks.title: Assistant, workflow or agent?
tasks.prompt:
Kiran’s family runs a kirana store in Nagpur. They want AI help with four jobs:
1. Write one Diwali offer message for their customers’ WhatsApp group.
2. Every evening, turn the day’s sales figures in a Google Sheet into a three-line summary for the owner.
3. Find the cheapest wholesaler for 20 items across Nagpur this week and place the orders.
4. Translate the shop’s price list into Marathi, once.
For each job, say whether it needs a chat assistant, a fixed workflow or an agent, and why. Then name one thing a person must check before the result is used. Hand in a four-row table. Last, paste the four jobs into a free AI assistant and ask it to classify them. Note one place where you and the AI disagree, and who is right.
tasks.hint: Ask two questions. Does the job happen once or again and again? Does the AI need to choose its own steps and tools? Only one job needs an agent, and that one shouldn’t place orders without the owner’s OK.
tasks.after: A strong answer: 1 and 4 are one-off jobs for a chat assistant (check the offer details; a fluent Marathi reader checks the list). 2 repeats on fixed steps, so it is a workflow (check the totals against the sheet). 3 needs an agent, because it must search and choose its own steps, and a person approves every order before it is placed.

reflection.prompt: Think of the last time you used AI, or saw someone use it. Which step of decide, brief, check and own was skipped, and what could have gone wrong?
reflection.hint: Most people skip the check. Be specific: name the fact, number or claim nobody tested.

workbook.hook: AI writes like an expert and guesses like a stranger. Learn to tell which one you’re getting.
idea: An AI assistant predicts likely words. That makes it a fast, fluent helper for drafts and explanations. It also makes it a risky source of facts it has never seen.
A workflow is a set of steps people fix in advance, with AI doing some of them. An agent chooses its own steps and tools. More freedom means more to check.
Whatever you use, the loop is the same: decide, brief, check, own.
why: You pick the simplest set-up that does the job
You know where errors hide before they reach anyone
Employers want people who check AI, not just use it
workbook.simple: An AI assistant is like a well-read new helper at a sweet shop on day one. He talks well about sweets in general. But he doesn’t know your prices until you tell him, and he may guess rather than say “I don’t know”.

myth.wrong: If an AI answers confidently, it has checked its facts.
myth.right: Confidence is only its writing style. It can be fluent and wrong in the same sentence, so you do the checking.

example.title: A hostel mess notice
example.body: Imagine Priya, the mess secretary at a hostel in Bhopal. She gives an AI the new meal times and asks for a short, polite notice in English and Hindi. The draft reads well. But the Hindi version says 7:30 where she wrote 7:00. She catches it because she reads both versions against her own note before posting. Decide, brief, check, own: five minutes, and no hungry students at the wrong time.

terms.meaning: The engine behind an AI assistant: it predicts likely next words from what it learned.
A confident AI answer that is false or made up.
Steps people fix in advance, where AI does some of the steps.
An AI that chooses its own steps and tools to finish a goal.
Something an AI can use beyond writing, such as web search, a file or an app.
A person who checks or approves before the result is used.

try_it.title: Catch a confident guess
try_it.prompt: I run a small tea stall in Indore. What was my total sale last Tuesday?
try_it.look_for: Does it say it can’t know, or does it give a number or a made-up method?
try_it.check: It has no access to your sales, so any number is a guess. Now ask: “What would you need from me to answer this?” A good reply lists what it needs instead of guessing.

try_it.title: See what it does well
try_it.prompt: Explain the difference between a workflow and an AI agent to a first-year college student, in 5 short lines, with one example from a small Indian shop.
try_it.look_for: Is it clear and short? Does the example match the definitions?
try_it.check: Compare it with this module: in a workflow, people fix the steps; an agent chooses its own. If the reply blurs the two, tell it which line is wrong and ask it to fix that line.

workbook.tip: Before you ask AI anything, say in one line how you’ll check its answer. If you can’t name a check, be careful with the answer.
workbook.mistake: Asking AI about facts only you or your organisation know, such as your fees, stock or timetable, and trusting the reply.

checks.scenario: A college fest team asks a free AI assistant, “How many students registered for our fest yesterday?” They attach nothing. It replies with an exact number.
checks.question: What is that number worth?
options: A guess: it hasn’t seen their list, so it gave a likely number
A close guess, since it has read about many fests of their size
A fair estimate, once they tell it how many came last year
A reliable count, if its web search was on when it replied
checks.hint: Card 1: how does an assistant produce an answer, and what can it not know about you?
checks.why: The assistant hasn’t seen the team’s form, so the number is a prediction written to sound sure. Other fests tell it nothing about theirs. Last year’s figure would make a better guess, but still a guess. Web search can’t see a private registration list. The real count is in their own form or sheet.

checks.scenario: A clinic sets up a process. Each new appointment request goes to an AI that drafts a confirmation message. The receptionist reads it and sends it.
checks.question: What kind of set-up is this?
options: An agent, because the AI writes every one of the messages by itself
A workflow, because people fixed the steps and a person approves
A chat assistant, because a person reads each message before it goes
An agent, because it runs again each time a request comes in
checks.hint: Who decided the steps: the clinic, or the AI?
checks.why: The clinic fixed the steps in advance and the AI does one of them, so it is a workflow. An agent would choose its own steps and tools. Running often doesn’t make something an agent.

checks.scenario: Nisha sends an AI-drafted email to a paper supplier. It asks for 500 reams instead of 50, and the supplier delivers 500.
checks.question: Who answers for the order?
options: The AI tool’s maker, since its draft had the error
The supplier, who should have queried so large an order
Nisha: she sent it, so the email is hers
No one: it was a software mistake
checks.hint: Card 3: whose name goes on what you send?
checks.why: Own means you answer for whatever you send, however it was drafted. The tool only suggested words; Nisha chose to send them. The supplier did what the email asked, and a mistake in a sent email is never no one’s.

quiz.title: The Monday booking summary
quiz.scenario: Debashis manages a co-working space in Kolkata. Every Monday he turns last week’s booking sheet into a five-line note for the owner, always under the same three headings. The owner wants written lines, not a table. Debashis wants it ready each Monday without starting it himself, and he will check the totals.
quiz.question: Which set-up fits this job best?
options: A chat assistant: each Monday he pastes the sheet and his saved brief, then checks
A workflow: each Monday the sheet goes to the AI, and he checks the totals
An agent: it reads the sheet, chooses what to report each week, and emails the owner
A Sheets formula: it totals each week’s bookings, with no AI step at all
quiz.explanation: The steps never change, and he wants it to run without starting it himself, so a fixed workflow fits. He still checks the totals before the owner sees them.
quiz.why_wrong: A chat with a saved brief works for a job you start yourself, but he wants it ready without starting it. An agent suits work whose steps can’t be planned, and these three headings never change. A formula gives totals, but the owner wants a written note, which needs the AI step.
quiz.learning_outcome: The facts of the job decide between an assistant, a workflow, an agent or no AI.

quiz.title: The student trip planner
quiz.scenario: A travel start-up in Kochi plans about 40 three-day trips a month for college groups. For each trip, the AI must find trains, compare hostels and check which sights are open. When a hostel is full the plan changes, so the next search depends on what it finds. Staff have no time to steer each search, and a staff member approves every booking.
quiz.question: Which set-up fits this job best?
options: An agent that picks its next search from what it finds, and books within budget
A fixed workflow: the same five searches in order; staff approve bookings
An agent that picks its next search from what it finds; staff approve bookings
A fixed workflow: the same five searches in order, then it books within budget
quiz.explanation: The next step depends on what each search finds, so the steps can’t be planned in advance. That is the job an agent is for, and staff approval keeps a person on the step that spends money.
quiz.why_wrong: An agent that books on its own would suit a firm that allows it, but here staff approve every booking. A fixed workflow suits trips that always run the same way, but a full hostel changes what happens next. A fixed workflow that also books on its own has both problems.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use an agent when the steps can’t be planned, and keep a person on the bookings.

quiz.title: The dhaba menu card
quiz.scenario: Gurdeep is printing 200 menu cards for his family’s dhaba in Amritsar tonight. He gave an AI his handwritten notes on 12 dishes. He raised every price this month, so his notes are the new list. The AI wrote an appetising line and the price for each dish.
quiz.question: What should he check before printing?
options: Every dish name and price, against last year’s printed menu
Four dishes at random, against his handwritten notes
Every dish name and price, against his handwritten notes
Four dishes at random, against last year’s printed menu
quiz.explanation: Prices are facts the AI copied, and it can change a number while sounding sure. All 12 prices are new this month, and any error is printed 200 times, so every line is checked against his notes.
quiz.why_wrong: Last year’s menu would be the right source if prices hadn’t changed, but every price rose this month. A random sample suits a quick, low-cost check, but one missed error here is printed on 200 cards. A sample against last year’s menu has both problems.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check every fact the AI copied against the current source.

quiz.title: The cough syrup message
quiz.scenario: Meenal interns at a pharmacy in Vadodara. She asked an AI to draft a WhatsApp message on cough syrup doses for children of each age. She sent it under the pharmacy’s name. The syrup’s label gives adult doses only. Neither Meenal nor the manager is trained to advise on doses.
quiz.question: Which step of the loop, done properly, would have stopped this message?
options: Check: compare each child’s dose with a dosing chart on a parenting blog
Decide: doses for children are a doctor’s call; the message sends parents to one
Brief: give the AI the label’s adult dose, to scale down by age
Own: the manager reads and approves the message before it is sent
quiz.explanation: Dose advice for children needs a doctor, so the Decide step keeps doses out of the message entirely. AI can still help word a message that sends parents to their child’s doctor.
quiz.why_wrong: A parenting blog isn’t qualified to set children’s doses, so this check would pass doses no doctor approved. Scaling an adult dose down by age is a dangerous guess, whoever does the sums. The manager’s approval adds a reader, but he isn’t trained to advise on doses.
quiz.learning_outcome: Decide first: health advice goes to a qualified person, not to AI.

modules.title: Briefing an AI well
modules.summary: The six parts of a good brief, the facts only you can give, and how to improve a reply instead of starting again.
modules.outcome: Write a brief with a goal, context, audience, limits, an example and a format, and improve it after reading the first reply.

learn.title: The six parts of a good brief
learn.body:
A prompt is what you type to an AI. A brief is a prompt that gives it everything it needs. Use six parts: goal, context, audience, limits, example and format.

Worked example. Weak: “Write an Instagram caption for our soap.”
Briefed:
Goal: get people to try our new neem soap.
Context: Rang Soaps is a small handmade soap brand from Jaipur. The soap costs ₹180.
Audience: college students who want simple skincare.
Limits: under 40 words, no medical claims, no more than 2 emojis.
Example: “Fresh from Jaipur, made by hand. Your skin will notice.”
Format: three options, each on its own line.

The weak prompt gets a generic caption, maybe with a made-up price. The brief gets three usable options. The common mistake is leaving out limits, then blaming the tool for breaking rules it was never given.

learn.title: Give it the facts only you know
learn.body:
The AI knows only what is in the chat and what it can look up. Your prices, dates, rules and product names must be in the brief. If they aren’t, it will fill the gap with something likely, and likely is not the same as true.

Worked example. A Raipur coaching centre asks AI to reply to a parent who wants a discount. With no fee facts, the AI offers “10% off for early payment”. The centre has no such offer. A better brief adds: “Fees are ₹18,000 a year. We don’t offer discounts. If you don’t know something, say the office will confirm.”

Also tell it what to do when it is unsure. In a long chat, the AI may lose track of early details. Repeat the key facts, or start a new chat with a fresh brief.

learn.title: Read, then refine
learn.body:
Treat the first reply as a draft. Read it, then say exactly what to change. Vague feedback such as “make it better” gets a random change. Specific feedback gets the change you need: “Cut it to 50 words”, “Use ‘you’, not ‘volunteers’”, or “Put the date in the first line”.

Worked example. An NGO in Lucknow asks AI for a message calling volunteers to a Sunday book drive. The first reply is 120 words and never says where to come. Round two: “Under 60 words. Put the place and time in the first line.” Now it works.

You can also let the AI ask first. Try: “Before you write, ask me up to three questions.” Its questions often show which facts your brief left out. The common mistake is starting again from zero instead of fixing one thing at a time.

tasks.title: Turn a weak prompt into a brief
tasks.prompt:
FreshTokri is a small vegetable delivery start-up in Pune. From 1 December, its delivery charge for orders under ₹299 goes up from ₹20 to ₹30. Orders of ₹299 or more still have free delivery. It wants a WhatsApp message to tell customers.
Step 1: In a free AI assistant, send the weak prompt: “write message about delivery charges”.
Step 2: In a new chat, send your own brief with all six parts: goal, context, audience, limits, example and format.
Hand in your brief, both replies, and two lines on what your brief fixed.
tasks.hint: Check each reply for the four facts: ₹20 to ₹30, under ₹299, free delivery at ₹299 or more, from 1 December. The weak prompt usually misses or invents some of them. Limits might include a word count and a friendly tone.
tasks.after: A good brief names the goal: tell customers clearly and keep them happy. It gives the four facts and the audience, regular customers in Pune. Its limits might be under 60 words and polite. It adds a short example and the format: one message ready to paste. Its reply keeps every fact right. The weak reply usually guesses.

tasks.title: Refine in two rounds
tasks.prompt:
You help the internship cell of a college in Mysuru. Final-year students must upload their CV to the college’s internship portal by Friday, 5 pm. Many haven’t.
Step 1: Ask a free AI assistant: “Before you write, ask me up to three questions you need answered to write a short reminder for these students.” Answer its questions.
Step 2: Read the reminder it writes. Give it one specific change.
Step 3: Give it one more specific change.
Hand in: the questions it asked, your two feedback lines, and the final reminder.
tasks.hint: Good feedback names one change and a measure: a word limit, what goes in the first line, the tone. “Make it better” is not feedback. Check the final version still says Friday, 5 pm and where to upload.
tasks.after: Strong work shows questions that found missing facts, such as the portal link and who to contact. Each feedback line asks for one measurable change. The final reminder is under about 60 words, with the deadline in the first line.

reflection.prompt: Which of the six parts of a brief do you usually leave out, and what happens to the reply when you do?
reflection.hint: Look at a prompt you sent recently. Most people leave out limits or the format.

workbook.hook: The AI isn’t reading your mind. It’s reading your message. Make the message do the work.
idea: A good brief has six parts: goal, context, audience, limits, example and format. Each one removes a guess the AI would otherwise make.
Facts only you know, like prices, dates and rules, must go in the brief. Then read the first reply and improve it one specific change at a time.
why: Fewer made-up details in the reply
Less time rewriting what the AI got wrong
The same brief can be reused by your team
workbook.simple: Briefing AI is like giving directions to an auto driver who is new to your city. “Take me home” gets you nowhere. “Near the bus stand, second lane after the petrol pump, I’m in a hurry” gets you there.

myth.wrong: There is a secret magic prompt that makes AI give perfect answers.
myth.right: There is no magic wording. Clear facts, a clear goal and a clear format do most of the work, and you refine from there.

example.title: A tiffin service changes its menu
example.body: Imagine Gurpreet, who runs a tiffin service in Ludhiana. She types “write about new menu” and gets a long message about dishes she doesn’t cook. Then she writes a brief. Goal: tell regular customers. Facts: the new Monday-to-Saturday menu, and the price, unchanged at ₹2,400 a month. Limits: under 50 words, in English and Punjabi. Format: one WhatsApp message. The second reply needs one small fix, and she sends it the same evening.

terms.meaning: Whatever you type to an AI.
A prompt that gives the AI everything it needs: goal, context, audience, limits, example and format.
The facts about your situation that the AI can’t know unless you tell it.
A rule the output must follow, such as a word count or “no discounts”.
The shape you want back: a table, three options, one message, bullet points.
How much of the chat the AI can hold at once; older parts may be dropped or summarised.

try_it.title: Run a full brief
try_it.prompt: Goal: tell students about a free study-skills talk. Context: our college library hosts it on Saturday at 11 am in Room 204; entry is free; no registration needed. Audience: first- and second-year students. Limits: under 50 words, friendly, no emojis. Example of our tone: “New books are in. Come and borrow one this week.” Format: one notice, then a one-line version for WhatsApp.
try_it.look_for: Does it keep every fact (Saturday, 11 am, Room 204, free, no registration) and every limit?
try_it.check: Tick each fact against the brief. Count the words. If it added something you didn’t give, like a speaker’s name, tell it to remove that line.

try_it.title: Let it ask first
try_it.prompt: I need to write a short message to my college’s NSS volunteers about a tree-planting drive. Before you write anything, ask me up to three questions you need answered.
try_it.look_for: Do its questions find facts you would have forgotten, like the place, the time or what to bring?
try_it.check: Answer with made-up but realistic details, then read the draft. Every detail in it should come from your answers. Anything else is a guess to remove.

workbook.tip: Keep your best briefs in a notes app. Next time, change the facts and reuse the rest.
workbook.mistake: Giving vague feedback like “make it better”, then starting again from zero when the reply changes the wrong thing.

checks.scenario: A music class in Shillong asks AI for a message about new weekend batches. The brief gives a goal, the audience (parents) and the format (one WhatsApp message). The reply invents batch times.
checks.question: Which part of the brief would fix this?
options: Format: ask for bullet points instead of a single message
Audience: write for the students rather than their parents
Context: add the real batch days and times from the class
Example: paste a message from a different music class
checks.hint: What did the AI have to guess because nobody told it?
checks.why: The AI invented times because the real ones weren’t in the brief. Context is where facts only you know go. Changing the format or audience doesn’t give it those facts.

checks.scenario: Arun must brief an AI for an invitation to his department’s farewell for a retiring professor. He has the date, but isn’t sure what else the guests will want to know.
checks.question: What is the best way to start?
options: Paste last year’s farewell invitation, so the AI copies its tone
Ask the AI to ask him up to three questions before it writes
Ask the AI to write it now and fill in likely details to fix later
Start a fresh chat for each draft, so no old guesses carry over
checks.hint: Card 3 ends with a way to find the gaps in your own brief.
checks.why: Arun doesn’t know which facts are missing, so letting the AI ask first finds them before it writes. Filling in likely details invites guesses he may miss. An example helps with tone, and a fresh chat helps in a long chat, but neither finds missing facts.

quiz.title: The yoga studio caption
quiz.scenario: A yoga studio in Bhopal briefs an AI for an Instagram caption. The brief gives the goal, the class times and fee (₹1,500 a month), the audience (working women), an example caption and the format. The reply is 140 words, has nine emojis and promises “guaranteed weight loss”.
quiz.question: Which part, added to the brief, would fix all three problems?
options: Context: classes at 6 am and 7 pm, ₹1,500 a month, women only
Example: “Stretch, breathe, smile. Your 7 pm reset is here.”
Format: three captions, each on its own line, hashtags at the end
Limits: under 40 words, at most two emojis, no health promises
quiz.explanation: Length, emojis and health claims are rules the output must follow, and rules go in the limits. The brief had none, so the AI broke rules it was never given.
quiz.why_wrong: The context line repeats facts the brief already has, and facts don’t set a length or ban a claim. The brief already has an example, and the AI still wrote 140 words, so another example won’t stop the promise. A new format changes the layout, and each caption could still be long and make the same claim.
quiz.learning_outcome: Rules the output must follow go in the limits.

quiz.title: Questions the fact list can’t cover
quiz.scenario: A tuition centre in Mangaluru uses an AI to draft replies to parents from its fact list. Parents ask about things the list doesn’t cover, and new topics come up every week. For these, the AI invents answers. Each parent writes in a new, short chat, and the tone of the replies is fine.
quiz.question: Which line, added to the brief, best fixes this?
options: “Here are our answers on hostels, scholarships and transport; use them.”
“Read our full fact list again before you answer every question.”
“If our facts don’t cover a question, say our office will confirm it.”
“Match the tone of these ten replies our office wrote last year.”
quiz.explanation: The AI fills gaps with likely answers unless told what to do when it doesn’t know. New topics come every week, so no list can cover them all; handing those to the office stops the guessing.
quiz.why_wrong: Answers on three topics would fix it if the gaps were always the same, but new ones come every week. Re-reading the list helps in a long chat that loses details, but these chats are short, and the list still lacks the answers. Example replies fix tone, which is already fine, and say nothing about gaps.
quiz.learning_outcome: Tell the AI what to do when its facts don’t cover a question.

quiz.title: Three hours, one chat
quiz.scenario: Ritika has used one chat for three hours to write product descriptions for a Jodhpur handicraft seller. Her first message said, “Prices include shipping. Never mention discounts.” An hour ago she reminded the AI of the rule in the same chat. Two drafts later, “10% off” came back. She has 15 descriptions still to write.
quiz.question: What should she do now?
options: Remind it of the rule again in the same chat, then redo the last few drafts
Keep the same chat, and delete any discount line from each new draft herself
Start a new chat with a fresh brief that repeats the key facts and rules
Start a new chat, pasting only the next product’s details to keep it short
quiz.explanation: In a long chat the AI can lose early details, and a reminder in the same chat has already failed. A new chat with a fresh brief puts every fact and rule back in front of it for the 15 drafts left.
quiz.why_wrong: A reminder in the same chat is the first thing to try, but she already tried it and the discount came back. Deleting the line herself works for one or two drafts, but 15 more means fixing the same error each time. A new chat with only the product details drops the rules, so nothing stops the discount there.
quiz.learning_outcome: When a long chat keeps losing a rule, start fresh with the full brief.

quiz.title: One wrong line
quiz.scenario: An AI drafts a three-line SMS for a gas agency in Nashik about its new booking number. The SMS fits in 160 characters, and the first two lines are right. The third promises “home delivery within 2 hours”. The agency makes no promise at all about delivery time.
quiz.question: Which reply to the AI fixes this best?
options: “Remove the line about 2-hour delivery; keep the rest as it is.”
“Change line 3 to say: Home delivery within 24 hours of booking.”
“Shorten line 3 so that the whole SMS fits in 120 characters.”
“Rewrite line 3 to say that our delivery is quick and reliable.”
quiz.explanation: The agency makes no delivery promise, so the line must go. Naming exactly which line to remove keeps the two right lines and changes nothing else.
quiz.why_wrong: A 24-hour promise would be right if the agency offered one, but it promises no delivery time. Shortening fixes length, but the SMS already fits, and a shorter line can keep the false promise. “Quick and reliable” is still a delivery promise, only a vaguer one.
quiz.learning_outcome: Feedback names the exact change the facts call for.

modules.title: Checking AI output
modules.summary: Why AI makes things up, four checks that catch it (source, claim, number, logic), and a verification log that shows your work.
modules.outcome: Find wrong numbers, invented sources and unsupported claims in an AI answer, and record each check in a verification log.

learn.title: Why AI makes things up, and where errors hide
learn.body:
AI tools sometimes state false things with confidence. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, published research in 2025 arguing one reason: training and testing reward a guess over “I don’t know”. So the model learns to guess.

Errors hide in the same places again and again: numbers, names, dates, quotes and sources. A made-up source looks real, with an author, a title and even a page number.

This has already reached Indian courts. The Bombay High Court ordered a litigant to pay ₹50,000 in costs for citing a judgment an AI had invented. The Supreme Court has called a trial court’s reliance on fake AI judgments a matter of “institutional concern”.

Worked example. An AI writes, “As the RBI said in its 2019 circular…”. Before you repeat it, find that circular on the RBI’s own website. If you can’t, the claim doesn’t go in.

learn.title: Four checks: source, claim, number, logic
learn.body:
Source: open it. Does it exist, and who published it?
Claim: does the source actually say this? Find the sentence.
Number: work it out again from the original figures.
Logic: does the conclusion follow from the facts?

Worked example. An AI summary of a Lucknow bakery’s accounts says, “Sales rose 20%, from ₹40,000 in May to ₹52,000 in June, so the new oven paid for itself.”
Number: (52,000 − 40,000) ÷ 40,000 = 0.30, so the rise is 30%, not 20%.
Logic: higher sales don’t prove the oven caused them. June might have had more weddings.

Use a second, independent source for anything important: money, health, law, or a fact you will publish. Another AI tool is not independent. It may repeat the same wrong page.

learn.title: Keep a verification log
learn.body:
A verification log is a simple table with four columns: the claim, how you checked it, the result, and what you changed. It takes minutes. It shows your manager, teacher or client exactly what you tested, so they can trust the work.

Worked example.
Claim: “Total sales were ₹2,10,000.” Check: added the six months in Google Sheets with =SUM. Result: ₹2,01,000. Change: corrected the total.
Claim: “Source: Retail Survey 2024.” Check: searched for it and found nothing. Result: unsupported. Change: removed the sentence.

A common mistake is asking the AI, “Are you sure?” It may simply agree, or change a right answer to a wrong one. That is not a check. A real check uses something outside the AI: the original data, the source itself, or an expert.

tasks.title: Find the planted errors
tasks.prompt:
Vidya Stationers is a shop in Hubballi. Its monthly sales for January to June were:
Jan ₹42,000
Feb ₹38,500
Mar ₹51,000
Apr ₹47,500
May ₹36,000
Jun ₹55,000
An AI wrote this summary of the figures:
“Total sales from January to June were ₹2,80,000. The best month was March, at ₹51,000. Sales grew 13% from January to June. May was the weakest month, at ₹36,000. The average month brought in ₹45,000. According to the 2025 Karnataka Retail Survey, stationery sales always fall in May because of school holidays.”
Check every sentence. Put the figures in Google Sheets (or use a calculator) to test the numbers. Hand in a verification log with one row per sentence: the claim, how you checked it, the result, and the corrected sentence.
tasks.hint: Four of the six sentences have a problem. In Sheets, =SUM gives the total and =AVERAGE the average. For growth, use (June − January) ÷ January. For the survey, try to find it and open it before you trust it.
tasks.after: The correct log: the total is ₹2,70,000, not ₹2,80,000. The best month is June (₹55,000), not March. Growth is (55,000 − 42,000) ÷ 42,000 ≈ 31%, not 13%. May as the weakest month and the ₹45,000 average are right. The survey claim has no source you can open, so it is unsupported and comes out.

tasks.title: Check the sources an AI gives you
tasks.prompt:
Ask a free AI assistant: “Give me 3 sources, with links, that explain how UPI works for a beginner. For each, quote one sentence from it.”
Open every link. For each source, record: does the page open, who published it, is the quoted sentence really on the page, and is it a primary source? (A primary source is the organisation itself. NPCI, which runs UPI, is the primary source for how UPI works.)
Hand in a log with one row per source, and one line on which source you would cite and why.
tasks.hint: Use your browser’s “Find in page” to search for the quoted sentence. A page that opens but doesn’t contain the quote counts as unsupported. If your assistant can’t search the web, it may give links from memory, so check them all.
tasks.after: A strong log opens every link and marks each one: works or broken, publisher, quote found or not, primary or not. It is common to find at least one link that is broken or doesn’t contain the quote. The best choice to cite is the primary source, NPCI’s own page, with the sentence found on it.

reflection.prompt: Think of a fact you once shared that turned out to be wrong, from AI or anywhere else. Which of the four checks would have caught it?
reflection.hint: Most shared mistakes are a number nobody worked out again, or a source nobody opened.

workbook.hook: AI can be wrong in a perfect sentence. Your job is to catch it before anyone else does.
idea: AI tools can state false facts, wrong numbers and sources that don’t exist, all in confident language. Fluent is not the same as checked.
Four checks catch most of it: open the source, find the claim in it, redo the number, and test the logic. Write each check in a log, so others can see what you tested.
why: A wrong number in your report is your mistake, not the AI’s
Fake sources have already cost people money in Indian courts
A verification log makes your work easy to trust
workbook.simple: Checking AI is like counting your change at the shop counter. The shopkeeper is probably right. You still count before you walk away, because after that, any mistake is your loss.

myth.wrong: If I ask the AI “Are you sure?”, it will catch its own mistakes.
myth.right: It may just agree with you, or change a right answer to a wrong one. A real check uses something outside the AI: the source, the original numbers or an expert.

example.title: The donor report
example.body: Imagine Arjun, an intern at an NGO in Chennai. An AI drafts the annual donor report and writes, “This year we served 1,200 families.” Arjun opens the NGO’s register. It says 1,020. He corrects the figure, and adds a line to his log: claim, checked against the register, wrong, corrected. When the director asks how sure he is, he shows her the log.

terms.meaning: Testing a claim against something outside the AI before you use it.
The original: the organisation, law, dataset or person the fact comes from.
Confirming an important fact in a second, independent source.
A source the AI made up: it looks real but doesn’t exist or doesn’t say that.
A table of each claim, how you checked it, the result and what you changed.

try_it.title: Ask for sources, then open them
try_it.prompt: Give me 2 facts about the history of Indian Railways. For each, give a source link I can open and the exact sentence on that page that supports it.
try_it.look_for: Do the links look like real pages? Is each quoted sentence specific?
try_it.check: Open both links and use “Find in page” to search for each sentence. If a page is missing or doesn’t contain the sentence, mark that fact as unsupported.

try_it.title: Do the maths yourself
try_it.prompt: A shop’s sales went from ₹25,000 in March to ₹30,000 in April. What is the percentage increase? Show your working.
try_it.look_for: Does it divide the rise by the March figure, or by the April figure?
try_it.check: Work it out: (30,000 − 25,000) ÷ 25,000 = 0.20, so 20%. If the AI says about 16.7%, it divided by the new figure. Tell it which step is wrong.

workbook.tip: Check the numbers and the sources first. They are where AI errors hide most often, and they are the easiest to test.
workbook.mistake: Trusting a citation because it looks complete, with an author, a year and a page number, without opening it.

checks.scenario: Megha’s AI-written assignment cites “Sharma (2021), Journal of Indian Commerce, page 45” for a key claim.
checks.question: What should she do first?
options: Ask the AI to confirm that the citation is real
Search for the article, open it and find the claim
Check the citation matches her college’s style guide
Keep it, since a page number shows the AI used it
checks.hint: Card 3: what must a citation pass before you rely on it?
checks.why: Only opening the article shows whether it exists and says what the assignment claims. The AI may simply say yes, and a neat format or a page number proves nothing.

checks.scenario: An AI says a club’s members went from 40 to 50, “an increase of 10%”.
checks.question: What is the correct increase?
options: 20%: the rise of 10 divided by the new 50
10%: the rise of 10 read straight as a per cent
25%: the rise of 10 divided by the first 40
125%: the new 50 divided by the first 40
checks.hint: Which of card 2’s four checks is this, and what does it tell you to redo?
checks.why: A percentage change divides the rise by the starting number: 10 ÷ 40 = 25%. Dividing by 50 uses the new number. Reading 10 as 10% mixes up members with a percentage. 50 ÷ 40 = 125% is the new size as a share of the old, not the rise.

checks.scenario: Two different AI tools both tell Sameer that his university’s hostel applications close on 30 September.
checks.question: Is that enough to rely on?
options: No: he should check it on the university’s own website
Yes: two separate tools agreeing means the date is checked
Yes: if both tools give a link, the date must be current
No: he should check that both tools gave the same source link
checks.hint: Are two AI tools really independent of each other?
checks.why: Both tools may draw on the same old or wrong page, so agreement, even on the same link, doesn’t make the date current. The university’s own website is the primary source, and it shows this year’s date.

quiz.title: The dairy’s August dip
quiz.scenario: An AI writes about a dairy in Rajkot: “Sales fell 25%, from ₹80,000 in July to ₹60,000 in August, because the new delivery app confused customers.” Rohit has checked both figures against the dairy’s accounts and redone the 25%: all correct. The AI gave no source for the cause; it inferred it from the dates.
quiz.question: Which check is still needed before this sentence is used?
options: Number: redo the fall as a share of August’s ₹60,000
Source: open the accounts again for July’s and August’s sales
Claim: find the page where the AI read about confused customers
Logic: whether the app, and not something else, caused the sales fall
quiz.explanation: The figures and the 25% are checked, but the sentence also claims a cause. A fall after the app arrived doesn’t prove the app caused it; the monsoon or a festival month could explain it too.
quiz.why_wrong: A fall is divided by the starting figure, July’s ₹80,000; dividing by August gives a wrong 33%. The accounts have already been checked, so opening them again adds nothing. A claim check needs a source to open, and the AI gave none; it guessed the cause from the dates.
quiz.learning_outcome: Once numbers and sources are checked, test whether the conclusion follows.

quiz.title: The census link
quiz.scenario: Kavya’s AI-drafted assignment gives a literacy rate for her district in Tamil Nadu. It cites the 2011 Census with a link, which opens a real table on the official Census website. The table lists the literacy rate for every district in the state.
quiz.question: What should she do before keeping the figure?
options: Keep it, as the link opens a real table on the official Census site
Check that the state’s total in the table matches the AI’s figure
Check that the table is from the 2011 Census, then keep the figure
Find her district’s row in that table and check the figure matches
quiz.explanation: A real link passes the source check only. The claim check asks whether the source gives this figure for this district. The table has every district, so she finds her row.
quiz.why_wrong: An official page that opens can still give a different figure, or another district’s. The state total is a different number from her district’s, so matching it proves nothing. Confirming the year checks the source again, not whether her district’s figure matches.
quiz.learning_outcome: A source that exists must also say the exact claim.

quiz.title: The fee total in the log
quiz.scenario: Manoj is checking an AI report for a coaching centre. His log row says: Claim: “Total fees this year were ₹3,40,000.” Check: “Totalled this year’s fee sheet with =SUM: ₹3,40,000.” The report goes to the director in ten minutes, and five other claims in it are still unchecked.
quiz.question: What should Manoj do with this claim?
options: Mark it correct, and move on to the five unchecked claims
Have a colleague add up the fee sheet by hand, to be sure
Mark it correct after comparing it with last year’s total
Mark it unchecked until a second person agrees with it
quiz.explanation: The check used the original data, and the total matches. With ten minutes left and five claims unchecked, the time goes to those claims, where errors may still hide.
quiz.why_wrong: Adding it up again by hand repeats a check =SUM has done, and takes time the unchecked claims need. Last year’s total is for a different year, so it can’t confirm this one. Waiting for a second person leaves a checked claim marked unchecked, and the report goes in ten minutes.
quiz.learning_outcome: Once a claim is checked against its source, spend the time on what is still unchecked.

quiz.title: Fifteen minutes to check
quiz.scenario: Pallavi has 15 minutes before an AI-drafted newsletter goes to 2,000 members of a cooperative bank in Thrissur. The branch manager checked the welcome paragraph’s member count and dates against the register this morning. The new parts are a quote the AI says is from the RBI governor and the bank’s two loan interest rates.
quiz.question: Where should she spend her 15 minutes first?
options: The member count and dates in the welcome, against the bank’s register
Every line of the piece, against last month’s approved newsletter
The quote and the two rates, against a news report on RBI rate changes
The quote and rates, against the RBI’s site and the bank’s rate sheet
quiz.explanation: AI errors hide in numbers, quotes and sources, and these are the new parts. Each goes to its own primary source: the RBI for the governor’s words, and the bank’s rate sheet for its own loan rates.
quiz.why_wrong: The welcome’s figures were checked against the register this morning, so they aren’t where the risk is. Last month’s newsletter doesn’t hold this month’s quote or rates. A news report is secondary, and the bank sets its own loan rates, so no RBI report gives them.
quiz.learning_outcome: Spend limited checking time on the new numbers and quotes, at their primary sources.

modules.title: Privacy and confidential data at work
modules.summary: What counts as personal and confidential data, what India’s DPDP law says, and how to share the minimum with an AI tool.
modules.outcome: Remove personal and confidential details from work data before using AI, and decide which tool, if any, may see it.

learn.title: Personal data and confidential data
learn.body:
Personal data is any data about a person who can be identified from it. Names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses, Aadhaar numbers, photos and health details all count. So do combinations: “the only left-handed bowler in the Class 12 team at our school in Kota” points to one person without a name.

Confidential data is business information that isn’t public: client lists, prices not yet announced, launch plans, salaries and passwords.

Worked example. A Surat textile trader keeps a sheet of customer complaints. It has names, phone numbers, order numbers and the complaint text. The names and phone numbers are personal data. Order numbers are too, because the trader’s system links each one to a customer. The complaint text may hide some as well: “Tell your driver Suresh to stop calling me at Flat 3B.” Check every column, including free text.

learn.title: What India’s DPDP law says
learn.body:
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (the DPDP Act) sets the rules for digital personal data in India. A business that decides how personal data is used is called a data fiduciary. It may process personal data with the person’s consent, or for certain legitimate uses the Act lists. The Act doesn’t ban using personal data; it attaches duties to it. Penalties for a business can reach ₹250 crore.

The Act doesn’t apply to an individual using personal data for a personal or domestic purpose. It also doesn’t cover data a person made public themselves.

The DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025. Most of their duties for businesses, such as notices, consent and reporting breaches, are due to apply from May 2027, 18 months after the Rules were notified.

Worked example. An intern pastes a client’s customer list into a free AI tool. She is acting for the business, not for a personal purpose, so that exemption doesn’t cover her.

learn.title: Share the minimum: remove, replace, use the approved tool
learn.body:
Before any work data goes near an AI tool, take four steps.
1. Ask whether the AI needs the personal details at all. It usually needs the pattern, not the person.
2. Remove names, phone numbers, addresses and ID numbers. This is called redacting.
3. Replace them with labels such as Customer A and Customer B, so the rows still make sense.
4. Use the tool your employer has approved. Your employer’s rules apply today, whatever date a law starts.

Worked example. Before: “Anita Rao, 90000 00001, order 7781: late delivery twice.” After: “Customer A: late delivery twice.” The AI can still find themes in the complaints.

Free tools differ in whether chats can be used to train their models. Look in your tool’s settings. The common mistake is removing names but leaving phone numbers, order numbers or details in the free text that still point to one person.

tasks.title: Redact a complaints sheet, then analyse it
tasks.prompt:
Rasoi Box is a tiffin service in Hyderabad. Its complaints sheet (all details invented) is:
1. Farhan Ali | 90000 00011 | Madhapur | Dal too salty twice this week
2. Lakshmi N | 90000 00012 | Kukatpally | Delivered at 2:15 pm, lunch break ends at 2
3. Rahul Verma | 90000 00013 | Madhapur | Box arrived open, rice spilt
4. Sneha Reddy | 90000 00014 | Gachibowli | Late again. Tell your boy Imran to stop calling me, I’m at Flat 402, Lotus Towers
5. Arvind K | 90000 00015 | Kukatpally | Same sabzi three days running
6. Pooja S | 90000 00016 | Gachibowli | Arrived 40 minutes late
7. Kiran Rao | 90000 00017 | Madhapur | Lid broken, curry leaked
8. Mohan Das | 90000 00018 | Kukatpally | Too oily for my diet
Make a redacted copy: replace names with Customer A to H, remove phone numbers, and remove any personal details inside the complaint text. Keep the area, since the question is about delivery routes. Then ask a free AI assistant to group the complaints into themes and suggest one fix for each. Hand in your redacted table, your prompt, the AI’s reply, and one line on what you removed and why.
tasks.hint: Row 4 hides personal data in the text: a staff member’s name and a flat number. Expect about four themes: late delivery, packaging, taste or oil, and repeated menu. Check the AI didn’t add complaints that aren’t in your table.
tasks.after: A good redacted table has Customer A to H and no phone numbers. Row 4 becomes “Late again, and the delivery staff keep calling me.” The AI should find themes such as late delivery (rows 2, 4, 6), packaging (3, 7), taste and oil (1, 8) and repetition (5). Every fix should match a real complaint.

tasks.title: Yes, after changes, or not here
tasks.prompt:
For each situation, choose: fine to use a free AI tool as it is; fine only after removing details; or not without your employer’s or the person’s permission. Give one reason each.
1. Improving the wording of your own CV.
2. Finding the average marks of 200 students from a coaching centre’s sheet that has their names.
3. Summarising a public government notice about exam dates.
4. Rewriting a client’s product launch plan that hasn’t been announced yet.
5. A friend forwards you her medical report and asks you to “ask AI what it means”.
Hand in a five-row table. Then take situation 1 or 3 and actually do it in a free AI tool. Hand in the output too.
tasks.hint: Ask two things each time. Whose data is it? Is it personal, confidential or public? Your own CV is for a personal purpose. A business’s data is not yours to share, even if you are using it for work.
tasks.after: A sound table: 1 fine (your own data, for a personal purpose; leave out your phone number and address anyway). 2 only after removing names. 3 fine, it is public. 4 not without the client’s or employer’s permission, as it is confidential. 5 only with your friend’s consent and with identifying details removed, and AI is no replacement for her doctor.

reflection.prompt: What personal data of other people is on your phone right now: contacts, group chats, photos? Which of it would you never paste into an AI tool, and why?
reflection.hint: Think of a family group chat or a class list. It isn’t yours to share, even though you can see it.

workbook.hook: Before you paste, pause. Whose data is this, and does the AI need it?
idea: Personal data is anything that identifies a person: a name, a number, a photo, or a mix of details that points to one person. Confidential data is business information that isn’t public.

India’s DPDP Act lets businesses use personal data with consent or for certain legitimate uses, with duties attached. Most of the Rules’ duties apply later, on dates set in the Rules. Your employer’s rules apply today.
Share the minimum: remove, replace with labels, and use the approved tool.
why: One careless paste can expose many people at once
Your employer, not just you, answers for a leak
Clients trust interns who handle their data carefully
workbook.simple: Pasting a customer list into a chatbot is like reading it aloud on a crowded bus. Maybe nobody writes it down. But it is no longer only yours.

myth.wrong: The DPDP Act bans businesses from using any personal data.
myth.right: It allows use with consent or for certain legitimate uses, and sets duties such as notice and security. Most of the Rules’ duties for businesses apply later, on dates set in the Rules.

example.title: The travel agency’s enquiry list
example.body: Imagine Farah, an intern at a travel agency in Kolkata. Her manager asks which destinations people enquire about most. The enquiry sheet has names, phone numbers and passport details. Farah copies only two columns, destination and month, into a new sheet. The AI finds the pattern just as well. No customer’s details ever leave the agency’s system.

terms.meaning: Any data about a person who can be identified from it.
Under the DPDP Act, the business that decides why and how personal data is used.
A person’s clear agreement to their data being used for a stated purpose.
Remove or hide details that identify a person before sharing.
Business information that isn’t public, such as client lists or launch plans.
The AI tool your employer or college allows for its data.

try_it.title: Practise spotting identifiers
try_it.prompt: Here is a made-up customer message. Replace every detail that could identify a person with a label like [NAME] or [PHONE], then list what you replaced: “Hi, this is Meena Iyer from Flat 4B, Lake View Apartments, Chennai. My order 55120 hasn’t arrived. Please call me on 90000 12345.”
try_it.look_for: Did it catch the name, flat, building, order number and phone number?
try_it.check: The order number can link back to Meena in the shop’s system, so it counts. This is practice on invented data only. With real data, redact it yourself before anything reaches an AI tool.

try_it.title: Find themes, then check one
try_it.prompt:
These five reviews of a Kochi bakery are already redacted. Find the two most common themes, and list which reviews support each.
A: “Cakes are fresh, but delivery took two hours.”
B: “Delivery was late again. The cake was fine.”
C: “Too sweet for me.”
D: “Lovely packaging, slow delivery.”
E: “Fresh bread and friendly staff.”
try_it.look_for: Does it list reviews for each theme? Does any theme rest on a review that doesn’t say it?
try_it.check: Pick one theme. Read every review it names. A theme counts only if each of those reviews really says it. Notice the AI never needed a name or a phone number to do this.

workbook.tip: Ask “Does the AI need to know who, or only what?” Usually it only needs what.
workbook.mistake: Removing names but leaving phone numbers, order numbers or personal details inside the free-text column.

checks.scenario: Divya, an intern at a Hyderabad cosmetics brand, wants a free AI tool to polish an email. The email gives the price of a lipstick launching next month, which isn’t public yet. It names no customers.
checks.question: What should she do?
options: Use the free tool, since the email holds no personal data
Remove any customer names, then use the free tool
Use the tool her employer has approved, or ask her manager first
Use the free tool, since the price will be public next month
checks.hint: Card 1 names two kinds of data to protect. Which kind is this?
checks.why: An unannounced price is confidential business data, so the approved-tool rule applies even with no personal data. Removing names protects personal data, not a secret price. It isn’t public yet, so “public next month” doesn’t make sharing it fine now.

checks.scenario: A college club is cleaning up its files before sharing them with an AI tool.
checks.question: Which of these is personal data?
options: A member’s mobile number, even with no name
The club’s total number of members this year
The club’s meeting day and room number
The average attendance across all meetings
checks.hint: Which one could lead you to one particular person?
checks.why: A mobile number identifies one person even without a name. Totals and averages describe the group, and a meeting day describes the club, not a person.

quiz.title: The courier feedback sheet
quiz.scenario: An intern at a courier firm in Ludhiana must send her manager the main complaint themes in each area within the hour. She has replaced names with Customer A to F and removed phone and tracking numbers. She has read every complaint: none names a person, an address or an order. The firm’s approved AI tool may see redacted customer data; her personal free account may not.
quiz.question: What should she do now?
options: Paste the area, date and complaint text into her personal free account
Remove the area column too, then paste the rest into the approved tool
Paste the area, date and complaint text into the approved tool now
Remove the complaint text too, then paste area and date into the approved tool
quiz.explanation: The identifiers are gone, and she has checked the free text too. The area and the complaint text are what themes by area need, so she shares them now, in the approved tool.
quiz.why_wrong: Her personal account may be quicker to open, but the firm doesn’t allow customer data in it. An area alone doesn’t point to one person, and the themes are needed area by area. The complaint text is what the AI must sort into themes, so removing it leaves nothing to analyse.
quiz.learning_outcome: Once identifiers are gone, share what the task needs, in the approved tool.

quiz.title: Three lists, one law
quiz.scenario: Three people paste a list of names and phone numbers into a free AI tool. Neel plans seating for his sister’s wedding from the family’s guest list. Ira, an intern at an insurance agency in Nagpur, drafts renewal reminders from the agency’s client list on her own phone. Joseph, a freelance wedding planner, plans seating for a client’s wedding from the client’s guest list.
quiz.question: Whose use does the DPDP Act’s personal or domestic exemption cover?
options: Neel’s and Joseph’s: both are seating plans for a wedding
Neel’s and Ira’s: both used their own phones and free accounts
Neel’s only: a family wedding is a personal purpose
All three: none of them sold or published anyone’s data
quiz.explanation: The exemption covers an individual using personal data for a personal or domestic purpose, like a family wedding. Ira acts for the agency and Joseph for his own business, so both are working for a business.
quiz.why_wrong: Joseph’s task looks like Neel’s, but he plans a client’s wedding as paid work, which is a business purpose. Ira’s own phone doesn’t matter: she is acting for the agency, not for herself. The Act covers far more than selling or publishing; it attaches duties to how a business uses personal data.
quiz.learning_outcome: The personal-use exemption depends on the purpose, not the device or the task’s look.

quiz.title: Not until May 2027?
quiz.scenario: In November 2026, a manager at an ed-tech start-up in Kolkata says: “The DPDP Rules’ duties don’t apply yet. Interns can paste student records into any free AI tool.” The start-up’s written policy says only its approved AI tool may see student data.
quiz.question: What is the best reply?
options: Right that most Rules duties start later, so a free tool is fine once names are removed
Wrong: the Rules applied in full when notified in November 2025, so no AI tool at all
Right that most Rules duties start later, and interns fall under the personal-use exemption
Right that most Rules duties start later, but our policy allows only the approved tool
quiz.explanation: Most of the Rules’ duties for businesses are due to apply from May 2027. But the start-up’s own policy applies today, whatever date a law starts, and it names one approved tool.
quiz.why_wrong: Removing names is good practice, but the policy allows only the approved tool, not any free one. The Rules were notified in November 2025, but most of their duties for businesses start later. The personal-use exemption covers individuals acting for themselves, and these interns act for the business.
quiz.learning_outcome: An employer’s AI policy applies today, whatever date a law’s duties start.

quiz.title: Which shift is off sick?
quiz.scenario: An HR intern at a textile mill in Coimbatore wants AI to find which shift had the most sick-leave days last quarter. The sick-leave sheet has one row per sick day: each worker’s name, ID number, phone, shift, date, and a reason that often names an illness. The mill’s policy allows its approved AI assistant for staff data once names, IDs and health details are removed.
quiz.question: What should she give the approved assistant?
options: Every column, with each name replaced by a label such as Worker A
Every column except the names, ID numbers and phone numbers
The whole sheet, since this is the assistant the mill approved
Only each leave’s shift and date, which answer the question
quiz.explanation: Shift and date are enough to count sick days by shift, and they hold no names, IDs or health details. That meets the mill’s policy and shares only what the question needs.
quiz.why_wrong: Labels hide the names, but the ID numbers and illness reasons stay, and the policy requires both removed. Dropping names, IDs and phones still leaves the illness reasons, which are health details. An approved tool still comes with the policy’s conditions, and the question needs only two columns.
quiz.learning_outcome: Share only the columns the question needs, within the tool’s conditions.

modules.title: What to hand to AI, and when not to
modules.summary: Judge each task by what a mistake would cost and how easily you can check it, follow the rules that apply, and keep the learning for yourself.
modules.outcome: Sort the parts of a real task into do it yourself, AI drafts and you check, or no AI, using the stakes, how checkable it is, and the rules that apply.

learn.title: Two questions: what if it’s wrong, and can I check it?
learn.body:
Before you hand a task to AI, ask two questions. Stakes: what does a mistake cost, and who pays? Checkability: can you easily tell whether the result is right?
Low stakes, easy to check: let AI draft, then read it.
High stakes, easy to check: AI may draft, and you check every line.
Low stakes, hard to check: use it with care, and label the result a draft.
High stakes, hard to check: don’t rely on AI. Ask a qualified person.

Worked example. At a clinic in Nashik, the receptionist uses AI to draft appointment reminders. A mistake costs little and she can check the date and time at a glance. Explaining a patient’s blood test result is different. A mistake could harm someone, and she can’t check it herself. That goes to the doctor, not to AI.

learn.title: When the rules say no
learn.body:
Sometimes the decision isn’t yours. Each college and employer sets its own rules on AI. Some allow it freely, some ask you to disclose it, and some ban it for certain work. For example, IIT Delhi’s 2025 guidelines require AI-assisted work to be fully disclosed. Exams, client work under contract, and confidential data often come with their own limits.

Worked example. Rhea starts an internship at a market research firm in Gurugram. Her contract says client data must stay in the firm’s own systems. A free AI tool would summarise the survey answers in seconds. She doesn’t use it. She asks her manager which tool is approved, and uses that one.

If you don’t know the rule, ask before you start, not after you have finished. “Everyone does it” is not a rule.

learn.title: Don’t hand over the learning
learn.body:
When the goal is to learn, letting AI do the work can cost you the skill. In a 2026 study by Anthropic, 52 mostly junior engineers learnt a new coding skill, some with AI help. The AI group scored lower on a quiz afterwards: about 50%, against 67% for those who coded by hand. Learners who asked the AI to explain kept more than those who handed over the whole task. A 2025 study by Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University of 319 office workers found that more confidence in AI went with less critical thinking.

Worked example. Diya is learning Excel formulas in Bengaluru. Instead of asking for the formula, she tries first. Then she asks, “Why does my formula give an error? Explain, but don’t fix it.” She learns the rule and can do it alone next time.

Use AI as a tutor that asks you questions, not as a machine that hands you answers.

tasks.title: Sort an intern’s week
tasks.prompt:
Aditya interns at an NGO in Bhubaneswar. This week he has six tasks:
1. Draft a thank-you email to 40 donors.
2. Total this year’s donations from a sheet for the annual report.
3. Translate a volunteer form into Odia.
4. Decide which of three families gets the NGO’s emergency support.
5. Write a social media post about a blood donation camp.
6. Summarise a 20-page government scheme document for the team.
For each task, rate the stakes (low or high) and checkability (easy or hard). Then choose: Aditya does it himself, AI drafts and he checks, or no AI. Say what he must check. Hand in a six-row table.
Then do task 5 yourself in a free AI assistant: invent the camp details (date, place, time) and write a brief. Hand in the post and your check notes.
tasks.hint: Task 4 is a decision about people’s lives, so it stays with people. For task 2, AI can help with the formula, but check the total in the sheet. For task 3, a fluent Odia reader must check. For task 6, the AI may skip a section, so check it against the document’s headings.
tasks.after: A sound table: 1 and 5 low stakes, easy to check: AI drafts, he reads. 2 high stakes, easy to check: AI may help, he checks the total in the sheet. 3 checkable only by a fluent reader. 4 high stakes and a judgement about people: no AI. 6 AI may summarise, checked against the headings. His post keeps the date, place and time exactly as briefed.

tasks.title: Learn with AI, not from it
tasks.prompt:
Pick a concept you are studying now. If you have none, use “compound interest”.
Step 1: Without any help, write three lines explaining it.
Step 2: Send a free AI assistant this prompt: “I am learning [your concept]. Don’t explain it yet. Ask me three questions, one at a time, to test my understanding. After each answer, tell me what I got right and wrong.”
Step 3: Close the chat. Write a new three-line explanation from memory.
Hand in both explanations, the three questions, and one thing you understand now that you didn’t before.
tasks.hint: If the AI starts explaining before asking, remind it: “Questions first, please.” Your second explanation should be in your own words, not copied from the chat.
tasks.after: Strong work shows a first explanation with a gap or a mistake, and three questions that probe it. The second explanation fixes the gap in the learner’s own words. For compound interest, it should say that interest is added to the amount, so the next interest is earned on the bigger amount.

reflection.prompt: Which task in your studies would you be tempted to hand fully to AI? What would you lose if you did?
reflection.hint: Think about the skill an employer would test you on in an interview. Is it in that task?

workbook.hook: The best AI users aren’t the ones who use it most. They’re the ones who know when to stop.
idea: Before handing over a task, weigh two things: what a mistake would cost, and how easily you can check the result. High stakes and hard to check means a qualified person, not AI.
Follow the rules of your college or employer, and ask when you don’t know them. When the goal is to learn, use AI to question you, not to do the work.
why: You avoid the costly mistakes that can’t be undone
You stay inside the rules of your college and employer
You keep the skills you’ll be tested on
workbook.simple: A calculator in a maths class is fine for checking. But if you never learnt what multiplying means, you can’t tell when you pressed the wrong key. And in some exams it isn’t allowed at all.

myth.wrong: Using AI for everything makes you faster and better at your work.
myth.right: Speed gains aren’t guaranteed, and handing over the learning can weaken your own skills. Use AI where a mistake is cheap or easy to check.

example.title: The group project rule
example.body: Imagine Sana, a second-year BBA student in Nagpur, starting a group project on a local dairy’s marketing. A teammate wants AI to write the whole report. Sana opens the course outline first. It says AI may help with ideas and grammar, with a note, but the analysis must be the group’s own. So the group uses AI to brainstorm survey questions. They write the analysis themselves and add a note on what AI did. Nobody has to guess the rule on the day they submit.

terms.meaning: Handing a task, or part of one, to someone or something else.
What a mistake would cost, and who would pay for it.
How easily you can tell whether a result is right.
Trusting AI so much that you stop thinking and checking yourself.
A college’s or employer’s rules on when and how AI may be used.

try_it.title: Sort five tasks, then compare
try_it.prompt:
Here are five tasks from my internship at a small travel agency:
1. A WhatsApp reminder of a tour’s departure time.
2. Telling a customer whether her visa will be approved.
3. Ten name ideas for a new weekend trip.
4. The total of advance payments for a group booking.
5. Explaining an airline’s refund rule to a customer.
Sort each into low or high stakes, and easy or hard to check. Then say whether AI should draft it.
try_it.look_for: Did it put any high-stakes, hard-to-check task under “AI drafts”?
try_it.check: Sort the five yourself first, then compare. For each disagreement, decide who is right using card 1’s four boxes. Only the embassy decides a visa, so nobody should promise one.

try_it.title: When it should say “ask someone”
try_it.prompt: My landlord in Pune wants to keep my full ₹20,000 deposit to repaint the flat. Is that legal? Answer in three lines.
try_it.look_for: Does it give a firm yes or no? Or does it say it depends on your rent agreement, and suggest someone qualified?
try_it.check: Ask yourself: could you check its answer? If not, card 1 puts this in high stakes, hard to check. A firm answer you can’t check is a reason to ask a lawyer or a legal aid clinic.

workbook.tip: If you couldn’t check the answer even with time, don’t rely on AI for it. Find a person who can.
workbook.mistake: Copying an AI answer for homework you will later be tested on without help.

checks.scenario: Tanya, secretary of a college club in Delhi, has four writing jobs today. She will hand one of them to a free AI tool.
checks.question: Which is the safest one to hand over?
options: The club’s fee summary for the college office, each figure checked
A reminder of tomorrow’s meeting time, which she reads before sending
A welcome note in Japanese for two exchange students, which nobody checks
Advice to a member on whether the bond in her offer letter is fair
checks.hint: Ask card 1’s two questions of every job, not just the one that looks easiest.
checks.why: A meeting reminder costs little if wrong, and she can check it at a glance. The fee summary is checkable, but a mistake costs more. Nobody can check the Japanese note. Advice on a bond is high stakes and needs a qualified person.

checks.scenario: Vikram’s professor says this assignment must be done without AI. A friend says, “Everyone uses it. Just rephrase what it gives you.”
checks.question: What should Vikram do?
options: Use AI for the outline only, and write the rest himself
Do the assignment without AI, as the professor set
Use AI, then rephrase every sentence in his own words
Use AI, and add a note at the end saying he used it
checks.hint: Who sets the rule for this assignment?
checks.why: The professor’s rule decides it. Rephrasing or using AI for part of it still breaks the rule, and a note doesn’t make breaking it fine. Disclosure helps where AI is allowed, not where it is banned.

quiz.title: The surgery deduction question
quiz.scenario: Shreya interns at a chartered accountant’s office in Thane. A client asks whether he can claim a tax deduction for his mother’s surgery, and he will file based on the office’s answer. His papers are hospital bills; whether they qualify depends on tax rules Shreya can’t judge. An AI tool gives a confident answer in seconds.
quiz.question: How should this question be handled?
options: A qualified CA in the office answers it; the AI answer isn’t relied on
AI drafts the answer; Shreya checks each line against the hospital bills
The AI answer goes to the client, clearly labelled as a draft to confirm
Shreya answers it herself from the tax department’s own online guide
quiz.explanation: The stakes are high, since the client files on this answer, and Shreya can’t check the tax rule. High stakes and hard to check means a qualified person answers, not AI.
quiz.why_wrong: Checking against the bills would work if the question were about amounts, but it turns on a tax rule she can’t judge. A draft label suits low-stakes work, but the client will file on it. The official guide is the right source for someone trained to apply it, and Shreya has no tax training.
quiz.learning_outcome: High stakes and hard to check: a qualified person answers.

quiz.title: The sister club’s notice
quiz.scenario: A college club in Guwahati got a short notice in Kannada from a sister club in Hubballi about a joint event. No one in the club reads Kannada. The sister club’s contact is on a trek with no signal until next week. The team only needs the gist to plan its reply in its own chat this week. Nothing will be published.
quiz.question: What is the best way to handle the notice?
options: Use AI for the gist, and tell the team it is an unchecked draft
Use AI for the gist, check it with a second AI translator, and call it confirmed
Wait for the sister club’s contact to explain it next week
Post the AI translation in the team chat as the notice’s exact text
quiz.explanation: The stakes are low, since only the team’s planning depends on it, but nobody can check the translation. Low stakes and hard to check means use it with care, labelled as a draft.
quiz.why_wrong: Two AI translators agreeing isn’t confirmation: they can make the same mistake, and no one in the club can check either, so calling it confirmed is untrue. Waiting for the contact misses the week the team has to plan. Posting it as the exact text makes an unchecked translation look checked, so a wrong detail could slip into the plan.
quiz.learning_outcome: Low stakes and hard to check: use AI with care and label it a draft.

quiz.title: Essay and exam in one week
quiz.scenario: Ankita’s college in Pune allows AI in coursework if she says what it did. It bans AI in the take-home exam. This week she has a coursework essay and the take-home exam.
quiz.question: Which plan follows both of her college’s rules?
options: AI on the essay with no note, since coursework allows AI
AI on the essay with a note on its use; no AI on the exam
AI on the essay with a note; AI on the exam for grammar only
AI on both, with a note on each saying exactly what it did
